plan.theme: a retiring school bus driver's farewell talk to students about noticing small things and keeping a promise to arrive

payload.title: Rhetorical Analysis: A Bus Driver's Last Morning

prompt.scenario: Speaker: Wendell Prusak, a fictional school bus driver who has driven Route 9 for the Garnet Hollow Consolidated School District for thirty-one years. Audience: the students of Garnet Hollow Consolidated School, kindergarten through twelfth grade, gathered in the gymnasium for the last-day-of-school assembly in June 2019, with teachers and some parents present. Exigence: Prusak is retiring at the end of the day and has been asked to say a few words; it is his only chance to speak to all of his riders at once. Purpose: to persuade students that two unglamorous habits, showing up when promised and paying attention to small things and people, are the real substance of a good life, and to hand the route and its promise over to his successor.
prompt.task: The following is a farewell talk delivered by Wendell Prusak, a school bus driver retiring after thirty-one years on the same route, to the students of a small consolidated school at their end-of-year assembly in 2019. Read the passage carefully. Write an essay that analyzes the rhetorical choices Prusak makes to persuade his student audience that keeping a promise to arrive and noticing small things are worth building a life around.
requirements: Respond to the prompt with a thesis that presents a defensible interpretation of how Prusak's rhetorical choices serve his purpose.
Select and present specific evidence from the passage to support your line of reasoning.
Explain how the evidence supports your line of reasoning, with commentary that shows how particular choices work on this audience for this purpose.

sources.title: Remarks at the Garnet Hollow Consolidated School End-of-Year Assembly
sources.attribution: Wendell Prusak, driver of Route 9 for the Garnet Hollow Consolidated School District, farewell remarks to students on the last day of school, June 2019 (fictional speaker, school, and occasion)
paragraphs: Thirty-one years ago I was handed a key, a route sheet, and a bus that smelled like wet mittens, and I was told to be at the corner of Pell Road and the old creamery by 6:52.

Six fifty-two, because that was when a girl named Tansy would be standing there with her clarinet case, and if the bus came early she missed it, and if it came late she stood in the dark thinking nobody was coming.
I have thought about that girl almost every morning since.
You might expect a bus driver to talk about safety, or feet in the aisle.
You have heard that speech from me, I'd guess, four thousand times.
What I want to say instead is smaller, and I think it matters more.
A bus route is a promise.
It says: at this corner, at this minute, in snow or in a heat wave, somebody will come for you.
In thirty-one years Route 9 has broken that promise eleven times, and I can tell you the reason for every one, because a promise you break should at least be a promise you remember.
Here is the other thing the job taught me, and it took longer.
Drive the same seventeen miles twice a day for three decades and you would think the road goes gray on you, like wallpaper.
It does the opposite.
I know which mailbox on Lantern Hill leans a little more each spring.
I know the heron that stands in the drainage ditch by the Ferrante place, one-legged, like a man waiting for a bus of his own.
I know the kid in the third row who stopped talking in October and started again in March, and nobody announced either event, but both of them counted.
Small things are not small.
They are just quiet.
Now, I can hear some of you thinking that this is easy for an old man to say.
You have tests, and phones, and a future people keep asking about, and the heron will not get you into college.
Fair enough.
I will grant you that noticing a bird does not add a line to your transcript.
But I would ask you this: who do you want to be at fifty-eight?
Someone who arrived everywhere on time and saw nothing on the way, or someone who kept the promise and kept the heron too?
I don't think you have to choose, and that is my whole point.
Let me tell you about the morning I almost quit.
January, the ninth year, black ice on the creamery curve, and the bus slid sideways far enough that I saw the ditch and the ditch saw me.
We stopped a foot short.
Nobody was hurt; nobody even dropped a backpack.
I sat there with my hands shaking, and a boy named Augie Petrakis, maybe seven years old, leaned forward and said, very seriously, "You did good, Mr. Prusak."
I did not do good.
I got lucky, and I knew it.
But that boy had noticed me, the way I had been trying to notice all of them, and I understood that the noticing runs both directions and is worth more than the brakes.
So here is what I am asking, and it is not much.
Show up when you said you would.
Look out the window.
Learn one true thing about the person in the seat next to you before June.
That is the whole job, and I did it for thirty-one years in a yellow box with bad heating.
The new driver's name is Ms. Oyelaran, and she will be at Pell Road at 6:52.
Be there.
She is coming for you, and that, as far as I can tell, is the entire meaning of a morning.
sources.stance: Showing up when promised and attending to small things are the substance of a good life

rows.name: Thesis

descriptors.0: No thesis, or a thesis that only restates the prompt (for example, 'Prusak uses many rhetorical choices to persuade students'), or a thesis that summarizes the speech's content without claiming anything about how it works, or a thesis that argues a position on the issue (whether small things matter) rather than analyzing the speech.
descriptors.1: A defensible claim about how Prusak's choices serve his purpose, stated in the introduction or elsewhere. The claim may name specific choices (his opening anecdote about the 6:52 stop, his concession to the students' objection, the near-crash story) or may characterize the speech's strategy more broadly (for example, that Prusak turns the humble details of his job into proof that reliability and attention are a single discipline). It must be about rhetoric, not just about theme.

rows.task_specific: Acceptable theses must connect at least one identifiable choice or pattern to Prusak's purpose with his student audience. A thesis that names three devices with no claim about their function ('Prusak uses anecdote, repetition, and rhetorical questions') earns 0 unless the body or conclusion later supplies a controlling claim about function; graders should check the whole essay before scoring Row A.

rows.name: Evidence and Commentary

descriptors.0: Restates the thesis, summarizes the speech, or offers evidence unrelated to the thesis.
descriptors.1: Mostly general evidence (for example, 'he tells stories about students') or evidence that is quoted but not explained; commentary, if present, repeats the quotation or names a device without saying what it does.
descriptors.2: Some specific evidence from the passage with commentary that explains how at least one choice works, but the explanation is uneven: some paragraphs identify a device and assert an effect ('this makes the audience feel emotion') without explaining the mechanism, or the essay treats choices as a list rather than building a line of reasoning.
descriptors.3: Specific evidence for all claims, and commentary that consistently explains how the choice works on this audience for this purpose, forming a line of reasoning. May still miss how choices relate to each other or to the situation (for example, that Prusak speaks to children as young as five alongside seniors), or may lean on one or two devices.
descriptors.4: Specific, well-chosen evidence, and commentary that explains how multiple choices work together to build Prusak's purpose, with attention to the rhetorical situation: his retirement, his mixed-age audience, his lack of formal authority, and the handover to Ms. Oyelaran. The essay shows how one choice sets up another (for example, how the concession in paragraph 4 earns the right to the near-crash anecdote in paragraph 5, or how the 6:52 detail from sentence 1 returns in sentence 39 to turn the whole speech into a single kept promise).

rows.task_specific: Choices that count: the opening anecdote and the precise time (sentences 1-4); the fragment repetition 'Not 6:50. Not 6:55.' (2); the definition-by-metaphor 'A bus route is a promise' and the colon that voices the promise (8-9); the admitted count of eleven broken promises as ethos (10); the wallpaper simile and the reversal 'It does the opposite' (12-13); the anaphoric 'I know' catalogue (14-16); the aphoristic antithesis 'Small things are not small. They are just quiet.' (17-18); the concession and rebuttal to imagined student objections (19-25); the paired rhetorical questions (23-24); the tone shift into the near-crash story (26-33), including personification of the ditch, understatement in 'We stopped a foot short,' and the irony of 'I did not do good'; the closing imperatives (35-37); the handover to Ms. Oyelaran and the return of 6:52 (39-41). Commentary should link effects to a student audience and to the farewell occasion. An essay that discusses only the content of the stories without attention to how they are told should not exceed 2.

rows.name: Sophistication

descriptors.0: Commentary stays at the level of identifying effects on 'the audience' in general; or the essay attempts complexity through sweeping statements about society, childhood, or memory that are not grounded in the text; or the prose is ornate but the ideas are not more precise.
descriptors.1: The essay does at least one of the following in a way that is sustained rather than mentioned once: explains tensions or complexities in the speech (for example, that Prusak builds authority by confessing failures, the eleven missed stops and the near-crash, rather than by claiming competence; or that he addresses teenagers' skepticism and small children's literalness at once); situates the speech within its occasion (a retirement that converts a routine into a legacy and a handover); explains how a device works at a level of mechanism rather than label (why the exact time 6:52 does more than a round number would); or writes with a consistently precise and controlled style.

rows.task_specific: Reward essays that notice the structural return of 6:52 and Pell Road, the reversal in which the student notices the driver, or the way the speech itself keeps the promise of being 'smaller' than a safety lecture. Do not award for vocabulary alone or for a single sentence gesturing at complexity.

scoring_notes: Total score is A + B + C, out of 6.
Row B is scored on the essay as a whole, not paragraph by paragraph; one very strong body paragraph and two weak ones generally lands at 2 or 3 depending on whether a line of reasoning is sustained.
An essay that misidentifies a device by name (calls a simile a metaphor) but correctly explains its function is not penalized; an essay that names devices correctly but explains nothing is.
Essays that argue whether small things really matter instead of analyzing the speech earn 0 on Row A and at most 1 on Row B.
Students need not cover the whole speech; an essay that analyzes three choices deeply can earn 4 on Row B if it attends to the situation and to how the choices work together.
Quoting sentence numbers is not required, but evidence must be specific enough that a grader can locate it.

defensible_positions: Prusak persuades by making himself small: he defines his job through its humblest details and confesses its failures, so that his authority comes from attention and honesty rather than rank, which is the exact quality he is asking students to adopt.
The speech is built as a frame: the exact time 6:52 and the corner at Pell Road open the talk and close it, so that the speech itself performs the kept promise it argues for.

Prusak anticipates the objection of his oldest listeners (that noticing a heron is useless) and answers it not with argument but with a story in which being noticed is what mattered, turning a lesson into a reciprocal obligation.

By pairing catalogues of small observations with aphoristic sentences, Prusak gives children language they can carry away ('Small things are not small. They are just quiet.') while giving teenagers a counterargument to their own skepticism.
lines_of_reasoning: Opening anecdote and exact time establish the stakes of punctuality through a single child's experience; the 'A bus route is a promise' metaphor generalizes it; the admitted count of eleven failures makes the promise credible; the closing handover enacts it.

The wallpaper simile sets up an expectation of dullness that the 'I know' catalogue overturns; the antithesis in 17-18 compresses the catalogue into a maxim; the concession in paragraph 4 tests the maxim against teenage objections; the near-crash anecdote proves it from the other direction.

Tone moves from wry (wet mittens, four thousand safety speeches) to plain seriousness (black ice, shaking hands) to tender command (Be there), and each shift lowers the distance between the driver and the listeners.

rhetorical_choices.effect: Grounds the abstract value of punctuality in one named child standing in the dark; the specificity of 6:52 shows that reliability is a matter of someone else's lived minutes, not a rule.
The two fragments 'Not 6:50. Not 6:55.' mimic the exactness being demanded and slow the listener down to feel the difference a few minutes make.
Redefines a schedule as a moral commitment, and the colon lets the route speak its own promise directly to a child, in language even the youngest listeners can hold.
Counting his own failures (eleven in thirty-one years) and insisting on remembering each one establishes credibility through honesty rather than boasting, modeling the accountability he asks for.

The wallpaper simile voices the expected dullness of routine so that 'It does the opposite' can overturn it; the heron 'like a man waiting for a bus of his own' quietly links the natural world to the students' own waiting.
The anaphoric 'I know' catalogue enacts attention itself, moving from a mailbox to a bird to a silent child, so that noticing objects becomes training for noticing people.
Compresses the paragraph into a memorable maxim that children can repeat and that reframes 'small' as 'quiet,' a matter of volume rather than worth.

Voices the older students' likely objection in their own terms (tests, phones, college), grants its partial truth, then reframes the choice as false, which keeps skeptical teenagers listening instead of dismissing him.
Projects the students forward to his own age and makes them imagine two versions of themselves, turning an old man's advice into a question only they can answer.
The wry, easy voice of the earlier paragraphs gives way to short clauses and a near-disaster, signaling that what follows is the speech's real evidence and earning silence from a restless gym.
'The ditch saw me' makes the danger an adversary with eyes, conveying terror without graphic detail suitable for small children.
'We stopped a foot short' and 'nobody even dropped a backpack' hold back emotion so that the child's remark, when it comes, carries the feeling instead.
The adult rejects the child's praise ('I did not do good'), reversing the expected direction of the lesson: the seven-year-old's noticing becomes the model, proving that attention is reciprocal.
The shaking hands and the serious little boy supply the emotional proof that noticing is 'worth more than the brakes,' an appeal beyond logic aimed at listeners who have ridden that same bus.
Three short imperatives convert the speech into a doable assignment, scaled down ('it is not much') so no listener can claim it is beyond them.
Naming the successor and repeating 6:52 and Pell Road closes the frame begun in sentence 1 and hands the promise to the students as their side of the bargain: 'Be there.'

source_uses.usable_for: All evidence; students should cite specific sentences and attend to paragraph position and the arc from anecdote to maxim to concession to proof to charge.

common_pitfalls: Summarizing the stories (Tansy, the heron, Augie) as if they were the point, without analyzing how their telling serves the purpose.
Device-listing: naming anecdote, repetition, and rhetorical question in sequence with 'this makes the audience feel' as the only commentary.

Treating the audience as generic adults rather than a gymnasium of five- to eighteen-year-olds, which is what makes the plain diction, short imperatives, and concrete objects (clarinet case, backpack, mailbox) purposeful.
Missing the concession in paragraph 4 or reading it as Prusak agreeing that noticing is useless, rather than as a move that disarms the older students' skepticism before the near-crash story.
Reading 'I did not do good' as self-pity rather than as a deliberate reversal that credits the child's noticing over the driver's skill.
Ignoring the ending, where the handover to Ms. Oyelaran and the repeated 6:52 convert the speech into an enacted promise.
Writing about whether reliability and attentiveness are good values instead of how Prusak argues for them.

blueprint.theme: Reliability and attentiveness as the substance of an ordinary good life
blueprint.issue: Whether keeping small promises and noticing small things deserve a student's attention alongside tests and ambitions
stances: Prusak: punctuality and attention are one discipline and both are forms of care for other people
Imagined student objection (voiced in paragraph 4): small noticing is pleasant but useless for the future

devices.function: Opens with a specific child at a specific minute to make punctuality personal.
Route as promise; definition of the job's moral meaning.
Colon lets the promise speak in its own words.
Counted safety speeches and eleven broken promises give concrete, slightly humorous evidence of long service and accountability.
Wallpaper simile sets up reversal; heron simile ties nature to waiting students.
Maxim that reframes small as quiet; either-or framing later rejected.
Grants the teenage objection and dissolves the forced choice.
Projects students into their own futures.
From wry to grave as the real evidence arrives.
Ditch 'saw me' conveys danger for young listeners.
Withholds drama so the child's line carries weight.
Adult rejects praise; the child becomes the teacher.
Shaking hands and the serious boy supply emotional proof.
Long sliding sentence then 'We stopped a foot short'; final 'Be there.'
Three imperatives make the request actionable.
Speaks to students as 'you' and hands them the promise.
